## 1. Drift confirmed

The JSON confirms it, and the source backs it up. Six labels across three files:

| File | Labels | href |
|---|---|---|
| `src/components/UserList.tsx:7-8` | "**Delete** user" / "**Remove** member" | both → `/users/manage` |
| `src/components/TeamList.tsx:6-7` | "**Archive** team" / "**Delete** the seat" | `/teams/manage` / `/seats/manage` |
| `src/components/SeatList.tsx:6-7` | "**Remove** member" / "**Archive** member" | both → `/seats/manage` |

Three verbs (`delete`, `remove`, `archive`), three nouns (`user`, `member`, `seat`), and the drift is *intra*-file as well as inter-file — `UserList` uses two different verbs for the same href, as does `SeatList`. Those same-href pairs are the proof that these are one action, not three.

Note the noun drift (`user`/`member`/`seat`) is also real but stayed **below the reporting floor**: the `user` alias group needs ≥3 aliases each in ≥2 files, and only `member` appears in two. Don't read its absence from the JSON as absence from the code.

## 2. Canonical label set

Three verbs, three distinct meanings — don't collapse them into one, disambiguate them:

| Intent | Canonical verb | Reversible? |
|---|---|---|
| Revoke a person's access to a container | **Remove** | yes, re-invitable |
| Hide a record but retain it | **Archive** | yes |
| Destroy the record irrecoverably | **Delete** | no |

Canonical noun: **member** for a person-in-a-container; `user` is the account-level identity and `seat` is the billing unit — neither belongs in a list-row action label.

That gives the target state:

```
UserList.tsx   → <NavItem label="Remove member" href="/users/manage" />   (one item, not two)
SeatList.tsx   → <NavItem label="Remove member" href="/seats/manage" />   (one item, not two)
TeamList.tsx   → <NavItem label="Delete team"   href="/teams/manage" />
```

Each duplicate-href pair collapses to a single item — two labels pointing at one destination was never a copy problem, it was a duplicated control.

## 3. Refactor `SeatList.tsx` first

Three reasons, in priority order:

1. **Zero semantic ambiguity.** Its two labels share the identical href `/seats/manage`, so you don't have to decide whether "archive" means something different from "remove" — the code already asserts they don't. `TeamList`'s "Archive team" vs "Delete team" is a genuine product question; `SeatList` isn't.
2. **It's the anchor file** on both findings (`"file": "src/components/SeatList.tsx"`), so it's what `crimes explain crime_00009` and any diff-scoped re-run will point at.
3. **It clears both findings in one edit.** `archive` currently qualifies via exactly two files — `SeatList` and `TeamList`. Dropping it from `SeatList` puts it at one file, below the ≥2-file floor, taking the qualifying-alias count from 3 to 2 and dropping under the ≥3 threshold. Fast feedback loop.

Be honest about what point 3 means though: **the findings clearing does not mean the drift is gone.** `TeamList` will still say "Archive team" while `UserList` says "Delete user" — that's still two verbs for one intent, just now under the detector's floor. Finish `TeamList` and `UserList` on the same branch.

And one thing neither detector catches: `TeamList.tsx:7` renders `label="Delete the seat" href="/seats/manage"` — a *seat* control living inside the team component, cross-wired to `SeatList`'s route. That's the highest-value correctness fix in the fixture and it's invisible to the label detectors, which only compare vocabulary. Handle it when you get to `TeamList`.

## 4. How the two detectors differ here

`copy_ia_drift` is a **restricted variant of** `action_label_drift` — literally the same code path. `packages/core/src/detectors/copy-ia-drift.ts:30` calls `analyse()` exported from `action-label-drift.ts:71`, with the same `ACTION_GROUPS` catalogue and the same thresholds. One flag differs:

| | `action_label_drift` (crime_00009) | `copy_ia_drift` (crime_00010) |
|---|---|---|
| IA label signals | all kinds | only `jsx_*` (`action-label-drift.ts:91`) |
| `document_title` / `metadata_title` / `use_title` | counted | skipped |
| `navEntries` (e.g. a `NAV` array) | counted (`:100-112`) | skipped (`:99`) |
| `fix_shape` | "pick one verb per action; update labels uniformly" | "pick the canonical label; redirect copies to it" |

**On this fixture, that difference is worth nothing.** The two findings are byte-identical in every field that matters — same group `delete`, same three aliases, same file lists, same anchor, same scores (`severity 0.4`, `confidence 0.6`, `agent_risk 0.27`). The reason: every delete-group token in the repo lives in a JSX `label=` prop on `<NavItem>`, which the IA index classifies as `jsx_label` — inside `copy_ia_drift`'s narrow window. The one genuine nav source, `src/nav.ts`, contains only `Teams` / `Workspaces` / `Organisations` / `Admin Console` — no delete-group tokens at all. So the broader detector's extra input surface contributes exactly zero additional hits.

The two would diverge on a repo where a delete verb reached the IA index through a nav array or a `document.title`, and not through JSX. This fixture has no such case, so the pair is pure duplication: **one problem billed twice**, inflating `summary.total` from 11 to 12 and double-counting in the low bucket. If you want that reflected in the baseline, the fix is on the crimes side — have `copy_ia_drift` suppress when `action_label_drift` already fired on the same `(group, anchor)` — not on the fixture side.

Treat them as one item of work: fixing the labels satisfies both.
